title: Mexico (Taiwan) fact of the day - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Mexico now supplies 40% of US imports of AI data-centre servers, with $46.9bn of enterprise server sales to the US so far this year versus Taiwan's $53.5bn, and briefly overtook Taiwan on a monthly basis in May. Taiwanese manufacturers relocating assembly to Mexico have made servers Mexico's top US export ahead of autos and are single-handedly propping up a weak Mexican economy.

themes.theme: Mexico as the AI server assembly hub

insights.claim: Mexico supplies 40 per cent of US imports this year of the computer servers used in the data centres that power artificial intelligence.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Any tariff or trade disruption on Mexico now transmits directly into US AI capex costs and datacentre build schedules — a channel most AI supply-chain models ignore.
insights.quote: Mexico has quietly become a cornerstone of the AI boom, providing 40 per cent of US imports this year of the computer servers that are widely used in the data centres powering artificial intelligence.
insights.locator: Mexico has quietly become a cornerstone of the AI boom

insights.claim: Mexico is the second-largest provider of enterprise servers to the US so far this year with sales of $46.9bn, behind Taiwan's $53.5bn, and on a monthly basis Mexico became the largest supplier in May.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: The crossover point where Mexico outships Taiwan in AI server value has already been touched — watch monthly US import data for a durable flip in the assembly geography.
insights.quote: Mexico is the second-largest provider of enterprise servers to the US so far this year, with sales reaching $46.9bn, behind Taiwan, which sold $53.5bn, though Mexico became the largest on a monthly basis in May.
insights.locator: Mexico is the second-largest provider of enterprise servers

insights.claim: Servers assembled by Taiwanese manufacturers in Mexico are now Mexico's top US export, overtaking autos, which had dominated Mexican trade for decades.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Mexican export beta has rotated from the auto cycle to the AI capex cycle — a structural change in what drives the peso and Mexican industrial activity.
insights.quote: Taiwanese manufacturers are rapidly expanding factories in Mexico to assemble servers, which are now the country’s top US export, overtaking autos that dominated its trade for decades.
insights.locator: Taiwanese manufacturers are rapidly expanding factories

insights.claim: Servers and related hardware made up almost one-fifth of the $317bn of goods Mexico exported between January and May, more than double the same period a year earlier, pushing total Mexican exports to record levels and propping up an otherwise limp economy.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Roughly 20% of Mexican goods exports now ride on one capex cycle; a pause in AI datacentre spending would hit Mexican GDP and the peso hard with little offset.
insights.quote: Servers and related hardware made up almost one-fifth of the $317bn of goods Mexico exported between January and May, more than double the same period a year earlier.
insights.locator: The phenomenon is helping prop up Mexico’s limp economy

insights.claim: Taiwan has risen to become Mexico's third-largest trading partner, up from eighth place in 2022, after Taiwanese companies spent more than $1.6bn since 2020 on Mexican factories offering geographic proximity and tariff-free access to US tech buyers.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: The whole arrangement is a tariff-arbitrage structure: if tariff-free access to the US is withdrawn, $1.6bn of Taiwanese Mexican capacity is stranded and server costs reprice.
insights.quote: Taiwanese companies have spent more than $1.6bn since 2020 on Mexican factories that offer geographic proximity and tariff-free access to US tech giants spending hundreds of billions on data centres.
insights.locator: Taiwan, in turn, is now Mexico’s third-largest trading partner

insights.claim: Moody's Analytics' head of Latin America economics characterises the AI server trade as creating not merely collaboration but dependency between the AI-powered economy and Mexico.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Frames Mexico as a chokepoint in the AI hardware chain alongside Taiwan — relevant to any geopolitical stress test of datacentre supply.
insights.quote: It is really a new frontier of collaboration and even dependency on the Mexican economy when it comes to AI servers.
